source.title: AXRP Episode 38.3 - Erik Jenner on Learned Look-Ahead

record.tranche_reason: Reports experiments on internal look-ahead in a chess-playing neural network, extending evidence about look-ahead to a non-language-model setting.
record.gate_note: The transcript reports qualitative outcomes from the chess paper's experiments. It gives no numerical probe accuracies or exact ablation effect sizes. The few-puzzle branching experiment is explicitly described as an informal attempt, not a systematic experiment.
record.test_reason: An interview in which the first author reports results from his chess-network paper. Probing, activation patching and attention-flow ablations show the network represents and uses specific future moves. These are the study's own results on look-ahead beyond verse (V5), in a chess transformer.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. Jenner also says look-ahead was operationalized only broadly: specific future moves are represented and used, with no search tree found. He suspects that look-ahead in language models may look quite different.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a chess-board transformer and chess-specific probes, activation patching, and attention-flow ablations; it does not test language-model rhyme generation or its intermediate-text intervention.
record.method_sensitivity: Effects are not consistent across puzzles; the speaker says some filtered puzzles show no effect. Probe-direction ablation is not specific because random activation interventions can have similarly large effects.
record.problems: The transcript reports mostly qualitative outcomes without exact values or uncertainty estimates. Some filtered puzzles show no effect. The probe-direction intervention is not specific relative to random activation interventions. The branching-futures result was tried on only a few puzzles and was not made into a systematic experiment. The speaker says the interventions require interpretation and do not determine the underlying algorithm.
record.rows_left_out: No reported result meeting the row criteria was left out.

untested.parts: Multi-step reasoning in language models, Sokoban, and other architectures; only one chess transformer is studied.
Depth of look-ahead is not quantified. The speaker only speculates that heuristics sometimes make look-ahead unnecessary.

missing.what: Probe baseline: the same probe trained on a randomly initialized model. Stated in the text but not recorded as a baseline or control row.

record.verdict_notes: This is a secondary, qualitative report (podcast) of arXiv:2406.00877, with no numbers beyond rough examples. The verdict rests on the interview's descriptions; the paper itself should be read for effect sizes. The model is Leela Chess Zero.

versions.untested_parts: Rhyme-word representation and interventions changing the intermediate line in a frontier language model.
Decodability of tokens several positions ahead from a language-model hidden state.
Pre-caching or breadcrumbs in next-token-prediction language models.
Rhyme planning in open-weight language models using attribution-graph or probing tools.
Tests chess only; does not test multi-step reasoning or Sokoban, nor whether the mechanism generalizes to language models.
Does not test whether language-model look-ahead is shallow or incidental, or whether local next-token features or heuristics explain it.

rows.subject: chess-playing neural network
rows.operation_detail: Train a probe to predict future moves from network activations.

rows.subject: chess-playing neural network
rows.operation_detail: Patch activations from a corrupted forward pass into a clean pass, comparing the target square of the future move with other squares.

conditions.value: target square of the future move

rows.measure: Effect on the output of patching information stored on a square
rows.baseline: Average effect of patching the square with the maximum effect among the other squares in each position
rows.value: The average effect on the future-move target square is bigger than the average effect of the per-position maximum among the other squares.
rows.note: The interview describes this as evidence that the future-move target square is unusually important.

rows.subject: chess-playing neural network
rows.operation_detail: Zero one attention-map number that carries information from the future-move target square to the immediate-move target square.
rows.value: The intervention has a very big effect.
rows.note: The interview characterizes the affected attention head as moving information between the two squares.

source_check.correct: Controls are stated: zeroing all other attention-map entries in that head, or zeroing a random other attention head entirely, has a very small effect.

relationships.condition: Filtered chess puzzles with a single forced reply, in positions where effects appear
relationships.reason: Future moves are decodable above a random-init baseline (R1). Patching the future-move target square beats the per-position max of other squares (R2). Zeroing one attention-flow entry has a big effect versus controls (R3). Small targeted interventions cut top-move probability from ~50-60% to ~10% (R8). An informal two-path test shows OR-like evaluation (R10, R11).
relationships.display_finding: Future moves were decodable above a randomly initialized baseline, target-square patching exceeded every other square's effect per position, zeroing one attention entry substantially affected choices, small targeted interventions reduced top-move probability from approximately 50–60% to approximately 10%, and an informal two-path test showed OR-like evaluation.

relation.reason: The interview reports the author's experiments on whether future moves are represented and used to select the current move, including additional informal branching tests.

tranche.reason: The author reports probing and intervention results on internal look-ahead in a chess transformer, a setting covered by V5. This interview reports the same work as arXiv:2406.00877 rather than an independent replication.

source_check.notes: Treat the interview and arXiv:2406.00877 as overlapping evidence. Probability examples are approximate, branching tests are anecdotal, and absent intervention effects do not establish absent internal look-ahead.
